patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/hmm: reject shadow-stack mappings
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch rejects shadow-stack mappings in the Heterogeneous Memory Management (HMM) module to prevent devices from gaining write access to user-space shadow stacks on x86 architectures.

review_comments.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the patch does not explicitly check for shadow stacks in hmm_vma_walk_test() and requested a check be added to prevent devices from gaining write access to shadow stacks.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 02:55:36PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> HMM can grant ordinary device write access to a userspace shadow stack.
> On x86, pte_write() is true for a shadow-stack PTE, so a populated page
> can be returned with HMM_PFN_WRITE without taking a CPU write fault.
>
> Nouveau translates that flag into a writable GPU mapping.
>
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(). Use the existing
> unsupported-range handling: a requested fault returns -EFAULT, while a
> snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
>
> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
> Fixes: 54007f818206 ("mm: Introduce VM_SHADOW_STACK for shadow stack memory")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Cc: "Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM)" <ljs@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>

Thanks for doing the HMM side of this, LGTM and:

Reviewed-by: Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) <ljs@kernel.org>

> ---
>  mm/hmm.c | 3 +++
>  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)
>
> diff --git a/mm/hmm.c b/mm/hmm.c
> index 2f1e98c6b644..fa61ca59d927 100644
> --- a/mm/hmm.c
> +++ b/mm/hmm.c
> @@ -596,6 +596,7 @@ static int hmm_vma_walk_test(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
>  	struct vm_area_struct *vma = walk->vma;
>
>  	if (!(vma->vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP)) &&
> +	    !vma_test_single_mask(vma, VMA_SHADOW_STACK) &&
>  	    vma->vm_flags & VM_READ)
>  		return 0;
>
> @@ -607,6 +608,8 @@ static int hmm_vma_walk_test(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
>  	 * allow write access either. HMM does not support architectures that
>  	 * allow write without read.
>  	 *
> +	 * Devices must not gain ordinary write access to shadow stacks.
> +	 *
>  	 * If a fault is requested for an unsupported range then it is a hard
>  	 * failure.
>  	 */
> --
> 2.56.0
>

--
Cheers, Lorenzo

whether we can *actually* write to a mapped page.

Well, and we have HMM that reimplements part of GUP in ugly ways (sorry) that we
missed.

> We do reject GUPs to shadow stack PTEs with FOLL_WRITE, unless FOLL_FORCE is
> passed. The tricky thing as mentioned my others in this thread is that shadow
> stack memory *is* writable by userspace. But also the kernel should not treat it

>

>

> concepts. What if there was a pte_userspace_could_write() and a

Gah, nak,

pte_write() just says "something might be able to write to it".

If that's actually true depends on other factors. Like the access+dirty on HW
that manages that in software.

I repeat: *no code* in Linux besides core-mm should ever interpret "pte_write()"
as "cool, I can write to it". The exception is GUP and unfortunately HMM.

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Jason Gunthorpe
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Jason Gunthorpe noted that the shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear on x86, but pte_write() reports it writable because shadow-stack instructions can write to it; this allows HMM to set HMM_PFN_WRITE, which Nouveau and RDMA use for GPU and device write permission respectively, potentially allowing a device or RDMA peer to overwrite the process's shadow stack. He suggested adding details about this behavior in the patch description.

> > : requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

> that is far more common..

Thanks.  This?

On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.

Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

On Sat, 2026-11-14 at 17:01 -0800, Andrew Morton wrote:
> Thanks.  This?

BTW, this is not just an x86 thing. Arm and riscv have the same pte_write()
shadow stack behavior for the same reasons. Despite not having the
Write=0,Dirty=1 thing, which *is* weird. But they still try to prevent the
kernel from writing it via logic in gup, etc.

On Thu, 2026-11-19 at 12:05 -0800, Dave Hansen wrote:
> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
> > On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> > rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> > shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> > HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> > RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> > registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> > to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> > potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> > 
> > Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> > A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> This is a fun one.
> 
> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
> 
> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

We do reject GUPs to shadow stack PTEs with FOLL_WRITE, unless FOLL_FORCE is
passed. The tricky thing as mentioned my others in this thread is that shadow
stack memory *is* writable by userspace. But also the kernel should not treat it
as such

A false negative for pte_write() is dangerous when the kernel needs to decide
when to revoke access. (i.e. fork) I think a mistake there is somewhat worse
then missing an exotic way to cajole the kernel into writing to a user's shadow
stack like this. So I think pte_write() being true for shadow stacks is the
correct implementation.

But, maybe the problem is that pte_write() is doing the job of two separate
concepts. What if there was a pte_userspace_could_write() and a
pte_kernel_should_not_write()? Names would need some work...

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function __zone_watermark_ok_mt() to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, which takes into account the migratetype of the request when checking if an allocation can succeed. The function is used in several places where the caller needs to know whether the allocation will honor ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests. The patch also moves the declaration of __zone_watermark_ok() to mm/page_alloc.h and makes no functional changes yet, as it's a preparation for future changes that will make the high-order check respect ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag. When this flag is set, the check should not consider free pages from other migration types when allocating a high-order request. This change aims to prevent fragmentation and improve performance under memory pressure conditions. The patch also updates the compaction logic to take into account the new watermark check and ensures that allocations do not stall in compaction unnecessarily. As a result, the patch is expected to reduce the number of stalls and failures during 64K mTHP faults under swap pressure.

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dev Jain suggested renaming zone_watermark_ok_mt to a more descriptive name, such as zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc, to clarify its purpose and distinguish it from the existing zone_watermark_ok function.
review_comments.raw_body:
zone_watermark_ok_mt is a bad name, I am having a hard time figuring out when
to call zone_watermark_ok and when to call zone_watermark_ok_mt. Let us look at
what zone_watermark_ok answers currently, according to the comment above it:

a) "Return true if free base pages are above 'mark'."
b) "For high-order checks it will return true if the order-0 watermark is reached
    and there is at least one free page of a suitable size".

So there are two uses: whether we have enough free pages, then, whether
we have enough free pages *and* we can also allocate.

So let us do something like: we have zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc. It will call
zone_watermark_ok, which will only handle the watermark computation (so this is a
refactor for the code ending at if (!order) line in current zone_watermark_ok).
Then it will also scan the freelists for the correct order, correct migratetype etc.

Then at the callsite we clearly know whether we are just looking for enough free memory,
or whether we are looking for an allocation too.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed Dev Jain's concern that the patch's high-order watermark check does not honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT for callers that pass a high order, specifically kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's __compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). The author explained that these callers need to scan the entire free list without filtering by migratetype, which is not provided by the _mt() helpers. They are open to renaming the _mt() function.
review_comments.raw_body:
A count-only zone_watermark_ok() does not work for three callers that
pass a high order: kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's
__compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). They
ask whether the zone has a free page of that order regardless of
migratetype. They need the free list scan without the migratetype
filter, so neither of your two helpers fits them.

So the split is not count vs scan. It is the zone as a whole vs one
request, as the comment above __zone_watermark_ok() says. The _mt variant
is the one that takes the request's migratetype. Callers that only want
the count already pass order 0.

I am not particularly tied to the _mt() name, but _for_alloc() is a
mouthful.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: vmscan: tell direct reclaim the allocation is ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the direct reclaim process in Linux to pass the allocation's flags down to try_to_free_pages(). Specifically, it records ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT in scan_control and uses this information to determine whether a costly order can succeed. This change is intended to improve performance by allowing direct reclaim to take advantage of free pages that are not movable or reclaimable. patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue caused by the high-order watermark check not honouring the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag in memory pressure situations. The check currently counts free pages of every migratetype, leading to incorrect results and stalls in compaction. The patches modify the watermark checks to take into account the request's migratetype and skip free lists that cannot be used. This is achieved by passing the alloc_flags to try_to_free_pages() and modifying the should_reclaim_retry() function. zone_watermark_ok_mt is a bad name, I am having a hard time figuring out when
to call zone_watermark_ok and when to call zone_watermark_ok_mt. Let us look at

b) "For high-order checks it will return true if the order-0 watermark is reached
    and there is at least one free page of a suitable size".

So there are two uses: whether we have enough free pages, then, whether
we have enough free pages *and* we can also allocate.

So let us do something like: we have zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc. It will call
zone_watermark_ok, which will only handle the watermark computation (so this is a

Then at the callsite we clearly know whether we are just looking for enough free memory,

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)

review_comments.raw_body:
A count-only zone_watermark_ok() does not work for three callers that
pass a high order: kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's
__compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). They
ask whether the zone has a free page of that order regardless of
migratetype. They need the free list scan without the migratetype
filter, so neither of your two helpers fits them.

So the split is not count vs scan. It is the zone as a whole vs one
request, as the comment above __zone_watermark_ok() says. The _mt variant
is the one that takes the request's migratetype. Callers that only want
the count already pass order 0.

I am not particularly tied to the _mt() name, but _for_alloc() is a
mouthful.

--
